message.content:
The 19th‑century sculpture that most people think of when they hear “famous” is **Auguste Rodin’s *The Kiss* (1889)**.  It was the first of Rodin’s works to be exhibited in Paris, it captured the public’s imagination with its sensual realism, and it has since become one of the most reproduced and celebrated images in Western art.

Other 19th‑century masterpieces that rival its fame include:

| Sculpture | Artist | Year | Why it matters |
|-----------|--------|------|----------------|
| *The Gates of Hell* | Rodin | 1880–1917 (unfinished) | A monumental, mythologically charged work that pushed the limits of expressive sculpture. |
| *The Thinker* | Rodin | 1902 (based on 1904–1908 casts) | Though technically early 20th, its conception began in the 1890s and it became an icon of contemplative art. |
| *The Statue of Liberty* (pedestal and statue) | Frédéric Bartholdi | 1886 | A monumental public monument that symbolized freedom and became a global icon. |
| *The Venus de Milo* (restored) | Various restorers | 1800s restoration | The 19th‑century restoration and re‑exhibition of this ancient marble revived interest in classical sculpture. |

In short, while many works were influential, Rodin’s *The Kiss* stands out as the single most famous 19th‑century sculpture in terms of public recognition, influence on later artists, and enduring presence in museums and popular culture.
